results.summary: This design implements a simple XOR cipher in which an 8-bit key is loaded into an 8-deep shift register using a leading header of ones, after which input message bits are XORed with the repeating key and presented on the outputs. The key repeats every 8 bytes, and the documentation explicitly warns that constant-key XOR encryption is trivially breakable by frequency analysis and must not be used for anything sensitive. Testing consists of observing that outputs 7 and 8 are high after initialization, though the author notes this depends on the flip-flop power-up state and is not guaranteed. No external hardware is required, and the project is a small Wokwi-based educational demonstration of stream cipher concepts.

This project drives a 7-segment display from eight input switches, mapping each switch to a display segment. The documentation is extremely thin, consisting only of the phrase 'Simple 7 Segment display' and an instruction to click the reset button. It requires an external 7-segment display connected to the outputs. Because no logic, mapping or purpose is described, little can be said about what the design actually does beyond passing switch states to a display.

This project appears to instantiate four two-input OR gates, with each pair of input pins feeding one gate, based on the pin names or2 through or5. The documentation is essentially absent, saying only 'I will Figure it out' and 'Soon I will firgure it out', so the actual behaviour cannot be confirmed. The stated external hardware is an LED display, suggesting the gate outputs are meant to be observed visually. No test procedure or design details are provided, making this an unfinished placeholder rather than a documented design.

This design is a 1-to-4 counter built from a clock divider whose output and inverted output drive two flip-flops, producing four distinct states that combinational logic maps to the numbers 1 through 4. The eight outputs are labelled output 0 through output 7, though only four states are described, so the exact output encoding is not fully specified. Testing is done by pressing the simulation button in Wokwi. The external hardware field was left as the unedited template text, so no real external components are documented.

This is a puzzle game in which each of seven input switches toggles a corresponding segment of a 7-segment display together with its neighbouring segments, and the goal is to reach states showing all digits from 0 to 9. The inputs and outputs share the same segment labels TM, TR, BR, BM, BL, TL and MM, with the decimal point unused. It requires an external 7-segment LED display and seven microswitches wired to inputs i0 through i6 and outputs o0 through o6. The design is a compact Wokwi-based logic puzzle with clear wiring instructions but no discussion of solution strategy or internal implementation.

This project is a logic gate test in which eight inputs labelled inputa through inputg drive four outputs, with outputb described as the main output that lights when the input combination is correct. The documentation is vague, stating only that outputb lights together with a line on the opposite side when the combination is right, and no truth table or gate list is given. Testing is done by trying different input combinations, and the author suggests using a numpad as a convenient input source. No external hardware beyond the user's hand and an optional numpad is required, and the design's exact function remains unclear from the description.

This project is titled RGB PWM and described as a small PWM module, with eight input pins labelled as bits 7 down to 0 of a value and a single output pin. The documentation consists entirely of the unedited template placeholders 'Explain how your project works', 'Explain how to use your project' and the external hardware prompt, so no actual behaviour, clocking or usage is described. The pin naming suggests an 8-bit duty-cycle input driving one PWM output, but this is inferred only from the pin labels. No test procedure or external hardware is documented, and the project appears to be an unfinished template.

This project is described as a binary converter for numbers from 1 to 3, with two input pins that set the least significant and second bit of a binary number. The documentation is essentially absent, with 'Still have to find out...' for how it works and 'Testing sucks' for how to test, and the external hardware field left as template text. No outputs are listed in the pin table, so it is unclear how the converted value is presented. The design cannot be meaningfully evaluated from the available information.

This project creates blinking lights on its eight outputs based on the states of the input pins, running from a 2 Hz clock. The documentation is minimal, saying only that it creates some blinking lights based on flipped input pins and that testing consists of flipping some pins. No external hardware is required. The design is a simple Wokwi experiment with no further detail on the relationship between inputs and the blinking pattern.

This project is an example template with eight inputs labelled i1 through i8 and eight outputs labelled E0 through E7. The documentation is entirely placeholder text, with 'NO: Explain how your project works', 'NO: Explain how to use your project' and the unedited external hardware prompt, and the one-line description is simply 'nothing'. No behaviour, test procedure or hardware requirements are described. Nothing can be concluded about the design beyond its pin count.
